description.narrative:
The Open Government Partnership (OGP) is a multi-stakeholder initiative established in 2011, aimed at securing commitments from governments to promote transparency, empower citizens, fight corruption and harness new technologies to strengthen governance. OGP currently comprises 75 national and 104 local governments and thousands of civil society organizations. To become a member of OGP, governments must meet OGPs eligibility criteria, endorse a high-level Open Government Declaration, deliver a National Action Plan (NAP) developed through public consultations, and commit to independent reporting on their progress through the Independent Review Mechanism (IRM).
OGP launched its 2023-28 strategy in 2023, after a year-long consultation process with a large community of government leaders, public servants, civil society, international partners, media and others. The result is a renewed vision for OGP as a more political, values-based partnership rooted in specific actions, innovations, and ideas for more open and democratic governments that meet citizens expectations. OGPs mission as part of the new strategy is to inspire, connect, and enable an ever-growing community of reformers and champions from government and civil society to take action together. OGP will achieve this by pursuing five mutually reinforcing goals: Strategic Goal 1: - Build a growing, committed, and interconnected community of open government reformers, activists, and champions - Build a stronger, more political global coalition for open government - Invest in leadership development for reformers - Expand strategic alliances and partnerships to reinforce open government principles
Strategic Goal 2: Make open government central to how all levels and branches of government function and deliver on their priorities - Provide a flexible action framework fit for diverse contexts and needs - Support mainstreaming of open government at all levels and branches of government work - Be more responsive to windows of political opportunity
Strategic Goal 3: Protect and expand civic space - Encourage civic space action and cultivate champions - Enforce and periodically review OGP policies on civic space
Strategic Goal 4: Accelerate collective progress on open government reforms - Raise the bar on transparency, accountability, participation, and inclusion - Launch a Partnership-wide challenge to promote collective action on ten priority areas (more information on the Open Gov Challenge below)
Strategic Goal 5: Become the home of inspirational open government innovations, evidence, and stories - Develop, curate and share high quality content - Create spaces for people to share their stories and connect

Insatsen avser ett stöd till organisationen Open Government Partnership om totalt 45 MSEK under en treårsperiod 2019-2021.
Open Government Partnership är ett multi-intressent-initiativ som startade 2011 med syfte att övertyga regeringar om insatser för att främja öppenhet, stärka medborgarinflytande bekämpa korruption och använda gemensamt utvecklade metoder för att stärka samhällsstyrningen. Open Government Partnership består för närvarande av 79 nationella och 20 lokala regeringar och ett tusental civilsamhällesorganisationer. För att bli medlem i Open Government Partnership måste regeringar uppfylla de villkor som är uppställda, göra ett offentligt uttalande om öppenhet, utverka en nationell handlingsplan med hjälp av medborgarkonsultationer och rapportera utvecklingen med hjälp av den oberoende översynsmekanism som finns i initiativet.
Open Government Partnerships vision är formulerad som att "fler regeringar ska bli mer transparenta, mer ansvarstagande och mer lyhörda för sina medborgares deltagande med slutgiltigt mål att förbättra styrning och samhällsservice". Arbetet kretsar kring nationella handlingsplaner som tas fram i en gemensam process mellan regeringar och civila samhället. Open Government Partnership arbetar utifrån en strategi som uppdaterades 2016 och utgör vägledning för verksamheten. Strategin kommer att utvecklas under 2019 för att med utgångspunkt i nuvarande vision formulera vägar för att nå bättre genomslag fram till 2022.
Strategin omfattar följande områden: 1) Ökat fokus på medborgarcentrerad samhällsstyrning 2) Breddat gemensamt ägarskap för nationella handlingsplaner 3) Ökad ambitionsnivå och lärande 4) Stärkt kapacitet, koordinering och nätverk för genomförande 5) Översyn av incitaments- och regelstruktur 6) Stärkt varumärke och kommunikationsstrategi
Total budget för 2019 är ca 12,4 MUSD. Budgetarna för 2020 och 2021 är uppskattade till 13,4 MUSD. Total budget är ca 39,2 MUSD. Sidas bidrag utgör knappt 10 %.

The intervention concerns support of 45 MSEK during the three-year period 2019-2021.
The Open Government Partnership (OGP) is a multi-stakeholder initiative established in 2011 aimed at securing commitments from governments to promote transparency, empower citizens, fight corruption and harness new technologies to strengthen governance. OGP currently comprises of 79 national and 20 local governments and some thousand civil society organisations. To become a member of OGP, governments must meet OGP's elibility criteria, endorse a high-level Open Government Declaration, deliver a National Action Plan (NAP) developed through public consultations, and commit to independent reporting on their progress through the Independent Review Mechanism (IRM).
OGP is directed by a strategy for 2015-2018 that was "refreshed" in 2016 to more clearly articulate the vision and identify the best means to work for that. By early 2020 OGP will complete a medium-term planning process, with the goal of developing a three-year implementation plan and budget (2020-2022). This implementation plan will not lay out a new vision for OGP but will focus on collective results that are aimed to be achieved in three years and how this will happen.
The strategy focusses on the following areas: 1) Deepen citizen-centered gocvernance 2) Broaden collective ownership of OGP domestically 3) Raise collective ambition, peer exchange and learning across OGP countries 4) Strengthen capacity, coordination and coalitions for implementation 5) Review performance incentives and rules of engagement 6) Strengthen the OGP brand and communications strategy
The total budget for 2019 is about 12.4 MUSD. The budgets for 2020 and 2021 are estimated to 13.4 MUSD respectively. Total budget amounts to approximately 39.2 MUSD. Sida's contribution constitutes a little less than 10 % for each year.

description.narrative:
Please note that OGP has in their Final Narrative Report been reporting in relation to the so called Grant Objectives that were included in the Original Agreement with Sida from Sep 2019. They were:
Objective 1: Deepen Citizen Centered Governance Objective 2: Broaden collective ownership of OGP domestically Objective 3: Raise collective ambition, peer exchange, and learning across OGP countries Objective 4: Strengthen capacity, coordination and coalitions for implementation Objective 5: Review performance incentives and rules of engagement Objective 6: Strengthen the OGP brand and communications strategy
For the record, OGP has been operating in accordance with their 2023-2028 Strategy since 2023. Those five strategic objectives (SO1SO5) are mentioned above on page 3 in this Completion Memo and it is only for the Final Narrative report that OGP has organised their results differently. Since 2023, OGP has in particular been working to create a more political, people centered, and inspiring partnership to drive open government initiatives worldwide, tackle important challenges facing society, and build on successes and lessons learned from the community. OGP realised in their cocreation process for the new long-term Strategy that it was needed to invest even more in the reformers, the actual people
Examples of results achieved with each of the six so called Grant Objectives (from the original agreement with Sida): Overview with OGP's own highlights:
* OGP has helped civil society gain a permanent seat at the policy table, embed open government across branches and levels of government, and accelerated the adoption of policies in access to information, public participation, open contracting, and beneficial ownership transparency. OGP's greatest strength is its community of reformers, activists, and champions they are the engine that drives policy and country-level results across the Partnership. The OGP model is unique, and it works evidence shows that political leadership, multistakeholder collaboration, peer exchange, and accountability lead to impactful reforms.
* Supporting reformers despite democratic crises: Afghanistan The fall of the government in Afghanistan in 2021 and subsequent takeover by the Taliban was a major setback for reformers working on building democratic institutions in the country over the previous decade. The OGP process and platform had enabled notable change in Afghanistan prior to the fall, led by courageous reformers working on areas critical to healthy and thriving democratic institutions, including anticorruption, womens rights, justice, and access to information. Across many measures, they had been succeeding despite persistent corruption, a weak state, and foreign interference. Following the takeover, OGP received many requests to support those who actively worked on OGP and partner initiatives in Afghanistan, many of whom risked facing danger if they stayed in the country. In 2021, the OGP Support Unit, with partner support, swiftly led the financial, political, and logistical efforts required to evacuate as many of these reformers as possible and this was done successfully.
* Responding to a global pandemic: The COVID19 pandemic starting in 2020 presented pressing challenges for both people and institutions, spotlighting the lack of transparency and participation in health systems and emergency decision-making, as well as a rise in executive power crowding out citizen voices and civil society. To find and showcase pathways for open government approaches to COVID19, OGP launched Open Response Open Recovery in 2020, a campaign to ensure the values of open government were embedded in actions to end the spread of COVID19. In 2021, OGP added another R to the campaign: Open Renewal. For the campaign, OGP created an open space for the community to share where they see open government approaches to tackling COVID19, whether implemented by governments themselves or civil society, citizens, or the private sector. Drawing on over 450 crowdsourced examples, OGP created a guide for open government and coronavirus as a one stop shop with practical ideas, tools and resources on how open government can support tackling the pandemic, amplifying the work of domestic reformers and partners.
OGP also said, when asked by Sida how they can use their learnings from the pandemic in a possible new global crisis, that "they learned that countries with preexisting multistakeholder forums and institutionalized cocreation processes were better positioned to respond quickly and openly to Covid, underscoring that the most valuable crisis tool is infrastructure for reform" Furthermore, "Institutionalization of OGP within member country ministries has also become a priority for OGP in the years following the pandemic. When in person cocreation processes got delayed due to social distancing measures, OGP developed guidance for making timelines flexible, as well as taking co-creation processes fully online, a capability now embedded in standard practice among member countries. OGP created the COVID-19 "Open Gov Tracker" during this period, a real time data aggregation tool that scraped and centralized data from partner organizations to monitor government behavior across areas like civic space, surveillance, media freedom, and Right to Information (RTI) frameworks. This type of tool could be redeployed when and if needed in the future.The addition of Open Renewal in 2021 further reflected that crises must not only be managed but used as windows of opportunity to address deeper systemic governance weaknesses, which is a principle that guides OGP's approach to ongoing and future shocks. These tools are ready to be used again."
Objective 1: Deepen Citizen Centered Governance
On page 5 in the Final Narrative report, OGP reports: "Between 2019 to 2024, reformers cocreated and implemented 1,928 commitments across 250 action plans (both national and local), demonstrating the scale and productivity of OGP's cocreation model. The quality of cocreation dialogue has improved as well, with the latest round of action plans seeing the highest rate yet of government responses to civil society on whether their inputs were or were not considered during cocreation and for the first time, more than two thirds of OGP governments provided this response." Sida followed-up with asking OGP to be more specific on how many commitments that have been fulfilled and partially fulfilled during the period 201924 incl. to report and analyse which kind of commitments (anticorruption, inclusion, digitalisation etc.) that are potentially more successful and if there are any geographic regions or countries that have been more successful in fulfilling their commitments. OGP responded in their updated their Final Narrative Report (see p. 16-17): "The Independent Reporting Mechanism (IRM) at OGP assessed almost 1,400 national action plan commitments (1,347) for implementation during the activity period 2019 to 2024. Of these commitments, 93% (or 1,259 commitments) saw at least some progress in implementation, while 58% (or 776 commitments) were considered fulfilled, i.e., they were substantially or fully implemented during the action plan period. (Clarification: There are fewer commitments (1,400) in this figure since these are the once that were both agreed and followed-up by IRM.) As for OGP local commitments (on local levels in governance administration), the IRM assessed 83 commitments during the activity period. The rate of implementation of these commitments was similar to that of the national commitments discussed above. Specifically, 92% (76 commitments) saw at least some progress in implementation, while 55% (46 commitments) were considered fulfilled. In terms of Early Results, 33% of implemented commitments (15 oct of 46 commitments) achieved major changes to government practices." Please also note that for the local numbers, the analysis only covers commitments submitted between 2017 and 2019. This is because local commitments are no longer assessed by the IRM. Only the local pioneers the first local governments to formally join OGP received IRM assessments. Furthermore, OGP reflected on their methods and that some indicators that the Independent Reporting Mechanisms (IRM) uses have changed since 2020. They also highlighted that OGP commitments in Action Plans in different countries and regions are not equal. They differ in scope, sometimes significantly. This makes comparisons difficult, even within countries. For example, a commitment to enact a new freedom of information bill and a commitment to update a government website to meet accessibility standards are significantly different, making them difficult to compare. Despite these differences, commitments remain the most effective unit of analysis to understand how OGP is working, according to OGP.
OGP also reported, when asked by Sida, regarding the trends that they could see in regions, themes etc. on commitment implementation (Completion), OGP's research shows that rates of commitment fulfillment are strongly correlated with levels of income in the countries. Specifically, the difference in the implementation rate between the highest and lowest income OGP countries is more than 30%, even when controlling for other factors. Indeed, an earlier study found that the most common obstacle in terms of commitment non implementation is a lack of budget and technical capacity. Commitment outcomes (Early Results), on the other hand, are not correlated with income. OGP's research shows that the main predictor of early results is not implementation, but the ambition level of the commitments. In other words, perhaps unsurprisingly, well-designed commitments tend to produce the most early results.
OGP's latest regional research shows that OGP countries in the Americas generate both the most ambitious commitments and the most early results, with rates of the latter more than double that in other regions. There are a few possible explanations for this trend. First, OGP countries in the Americas generally have stronger cocreation processes and spaces for permanent dialogue than elsewhere in OGP, and the research shows that levels of public participation during the OGP process are linked to better reforms, including early results. Second, countries in the Americas have institutionalized OGP (i.e., they have established formal rules and procedures) to a greater degree than countries in other regions. This provides stability, continuity during political transitions, and a stronger foundation from which to develop ambitious reforms.
Regarding different themes of commitments An interesting insight from OGP data is that the level of completion, or fulfillment, of commitments does not vary significantly based on the thematic focus of commitments. In other words, implementation rates are relatively similar across different areas of reform, such as public services, anticorruption, and justice with the implementation rate of the most frequently addressed policy areas hovering between 50% and 65%.
* Regarding gender and inclusion: The OGP Partnership's focused advocacy efforts have driven significant growth in the area of Inclusion, with for instance the 2019 "Break the Roles" campaign, OGP's first integrated advocacy campaign, achieving nearly 40% of OGP members making at least one gender commitment in their action plans. This represented a watershed moment, with seven members making gender-related commitments for the first time and more than 20 governments and partners forming the OGP Gender Coalition to guide and amplify this work. Across OGP members, gender reforms have delivered concrete results for vulnerable populations, from establishing gender equality commissions that address rights violations and combat trafficking, to embedding gender perspectives into state development strategies and ensuring crossparty political commitments to women's empowerment.
OGP has also mainstreamed gender perspectives throughout its guidance and support, integrating gender across thematic areas. Multistakeholder forums (MSFs) have also become more inclusive, with 41% including representation of marginalized groups by 2021, most commonly women, LGBTQI individuals and communities, and youth. In most countries, representatives from women's' organizations also participate in national steering committee leadership or in multistakeholder groups.
* Anti-corruption commitments are among the most ambitious and most likely to generate strong early results across OGP, including areas such as beneficial ownership transparency (BOT), whistleblowing, extractive industries, audits, and open contracting. Evidence from OGP's first ten years shows that OGP countries making ambitious commitments in areas like beneficial ownership transparency and open budgets across multiple action plans have become more open than other countries across many measures according to third-party assessments. Beneficial ownership transparency, specifically, has become one of the fastest growing and most ambitious policy areas, with nearly 40 countries having included BOT reforms in their OGP action plans and growing from a single commitment in 2013 to more than 80 commitments today.
LESSONS LEARNED related to Grant Objective 1: At the domestic level, co-creation between government and civil society is in the DNA of the OGP model. OGP has defined and shaped what cocreation looks like in practice and how it improves policy making. This is one of the most impactful achievements of the partnership and makes it unique in the space of democracy and good governance initiatives. The policy areas featured here reflect OGP's bottom-up approach to reform they emerged from demand by local stakeholders and gained/maintained momentum through sustained campaign efforts, consistent funding, and strong partnerships. This combination of grassroots demand and strategic support has enabled countries to capitalize on increased political support while accessing the technical expertise needed for implementation.
Objective 2: Broaden collective ownership of OGP domestically * Institutionalized open government processes p.8 Over the past five years, OGP made a concerted effort to embed open government across branches and levels of government. Institutionalization, refers to the process by which policies, practices, systems or laws become embedded and sustained within the government. Over 75% of members now have institutionalized open government processes. This has ensured crossparty support and continuity of reform agendas through political transitions. For example, Philippines executive order backed OGP office showed how institutional mandates and resources can stabilize reforms through political transitions. Another example from Armenia where a new Participatory Governance Department within the Prime Ministers office cemented open government at the core of policymaking.
LESSONS LEARNED related to Grant Objective 2: A key learning from OGPs decadelong work is the importance of building stronger institutional and political buy-in into open government that could be sustained across administrations or other political shifts. Institutionalizing open government to go beyond only the executive branch is therefore essential and a key part of OGPs 2023-2028 strategy. OGP initially trialled the expansion of open government adoption across institutions in a handful of countries, working with existing reformers to identify and reach out to champions at local levels, parliaments and judiciaries who were not familiar with OGP. It took persistence and strategic relationship building to connect reformers to each other so they could see their complementary roles in advancing specific policy areas, rather than pursuing disconnected agendas through standalone processes.
Objective 3: Raise collective ambition, peer exchange, and learning across OGP countries * Mobilizing political commitment (p.9): OGP has held two global Summits and six regional meetings across all four OGP regions in the past five years, which have proven instrumental in maintaining political engagement. Although engagement from Heads of State has waned recently coinciding with democratic backsliding globally, OGP has successfully mobilized a broader spectrum of highlevel political leadership including members of parliament, judiciary officials, mayors, and ministers, particularly from the Global South standing at 60% in 2024. For instance, OGP's 2024 regional meeting in the Americas attracted eight high level judges for the first time, building a pipeline of future champions across institutions and ensuring that open government reforms are less vulnerable to being deprioritized when political leadership changes.
* Unique leadership model: OGPs Steering Committee is a unique governance structure leading the partnership with equal representation from government and civil society leaders from the global north and global south. The committee has evolved into a more political leadership role, with Brazil, for example, opening the door for OGP to participate in the G20 Anti-Corruption Working Group meeting and Armenia spotlighting OGP for its progress on beneficial ownership at the IACC.
* Strategic partnerships amplify impact: OGP does not advance open government reforms in isolation. Over the years, the Partnership has carefully built and leveraged strategic partnerships and coalitions to amplify open government practices worldwide. The network includes 35 Ambassadors and Envoys and 18 institutional partners who leverage their political capital to influence international agendas and reach new audiences. The Partnership's numerous active funders have also been critical partners in resourcing domestic reforms to ensure their effective implementation.
* Coalitions connect global platforms to domestic implementation: OGP has been the connective tissue between global platforms and agreements and domestic implementation. From shaping anticorruption guidelines of the European Commission, G20, and United Nations Convention against Corruption (UNCAC) to amplifying AI, climate, and justice at the OECD and UN Digital Compact, OGP has significantly influenced policy debates at the global level while grounding them in local reform. Since OGP's launch in 2011, it has convened 11 coalitions on policy issues such as civic space, youth inclusion, open algorithms, and beneficial ownership many at nascent stages and scaled them across the Partnership. Through these coalitions, forward-thinking government and civil society leaders, as well as those with proven track records in specific policy areas, take collective action on difficult reforms.
LESSONS LEARNED related to Grant Objective 3: OGP has also had to ensure that policy ideas that gain momentum at the global level don't lose traction at the domestic level. This is where it has been critical to build coalitions, and connect countries to their peers so that the practical knowledge and howto of a reform gets diffused across the partnership.
Objective 4: Strengthen capacity, coordination and coalitions for implementation * Beneficial ownership and strategical engagement (p.11): Nigerias progress on beneficial ownership reforms is a case in point it demonstrates how OGP strategically engaged political leaders, mobilized resources from multilateral funders, and built coalitions inside and outside of government to overcome challenges around budgeting, institutional memory, and cross-agency collaboration. OGP championed the central role of committed and influential reformers and invested in their leadership skills. For example, OGP profiled then Minister of State, Budget and National Planning and Nigerian OGP Co-Chair Clem Agba and Registrar General Alhaji Abubakar Garba in regional and global OGP events and stories. Agbas leadership and influence proved critical in having Nigerias membership in the Beneficial Ownership Leadership Group officially approved by President Buhari.
*Since 2020, OGP has also resourced civil society with close to USD $2 million to support their engagement in OGP processes and reforms. A large proportion of these funds have supported CSOs in the Eastern Partnership Region (Ukraine, Armenia, Georgia, and Moldova) while the largest number of grantees supported were in the Africa and the Middle East Region (20 CSOs). This support has had a tangible impact on strengthening government -civil society dialogue and engaging the general public in government policies.
LESSONS LEARNED related to Grant Objective 4: While OGPs early years were focused in developing guidance and encouraging uptake on cocreation from its members, this began to shift with an equal focus on investing in the people and their skills. There came a realization that the lifeblood of the platform were its reformers both from inside the government as well as outside who were passionate about open government. Their political astuteness, subject matter expertise and commitment to the cause were critical enablers in any reform process and could either make or break country level progress. This understanding led OGP to develop specific tools and resources to support reformers as individuals as well as in groups. In every successful reform whether it was Nigerias beneficial ownership transparency reforms or Ukraine's open contracting platform there were champions working in their individual capacity as well as part of a strong coalition to drive progress. OGP in concert with its strategic partners has consistently provided political and technical knowhow, resources and recognition to reformers and will continue to do so as a central part of its strategy.
Objective 5: Review performance incentives and rules of engagement
Since 2019, the OGP platform has evolved to become more responsive to the needs and contexts of its members. The OGP Support Unit has implemented a more flexible action framework and more comprehensive member services. As a result, the OGP platform has generated greater stakeholder engagement and more widespread adoption of open government reforms. * Introducing flexible rules to allow for greater engagement OGP Local scaled tenfold (p.13): In 2020, OGP launched a new OGP Local program that made it easier for local governments to join and engage in OGP. OGP unveiled new innovations such as flexible action plans, rolling commitments, e-filing, and local led monitoring bodies. The result has been an expanded coalition of committed local reformers. OGP Local scaled tenfold from 15 members in 2019 to 151 in 2024.
* A new initiative spurs ambition: At the 2023 OGP Summit in Estonia, OGP launched the Open Gov Challenge, a new avenue for institutions at any level or branch of government to submit commitments to address key areas of open government. Adoption since has been widespread. By the 2025 OGP Summit in Spain, 65 governments in 42 countries had made more than 150 Challenge commitments. And these commitments matter OGPs Independent Reporting Mechanism (IRM) has found that these commitments are among the most ambitious in OGP.
* Independent Reporting Mechanism (IRM) refresh leads to better learning: In 2020, the OGP Steering Committee approved the IRM Refresh, a new approach to the IRM aimed to increase adoption of IRM findings and recommendations. This included the launch of IRM Co-Creation Briefs with recommendations for policy areas to consider during cocreation, which early evidence shows is linked to government adoption of new policy areas (brief forthcoming). OGP research also finds that OGP governments are implementing about half of all IRM recommendations, and that doing so is associated with higher quality action plans and processes.
LESSONS LEARNED related to Grant Objective 5: OGPs latest strategic plan for 202328 was the result of the largest community consultation held over a year, and one of the key pieces of stakeholder feedback was the need to adapt rules and incentives for the partnership to fit a diversity of contexts. This was a big shift in the current operating framework of the partnership as allowing action plans with different timeframes also had knock on effects on how the IRM would measure progress over time and across countries. As the changes are being adopted across members, there has been a noticeable increase in the engagement of new actors at both national and local levels. Anecdotally, OGP has also received feedback expressing greater satisfaction with the implementation of the new strategy.
Objective 6: Strengthen the OGP brand and communications strategy * As OGPs strategy shifted from a focus on amplifying reforms to supporting reformers, its communications strategy also aligned with this shift during the period of 20182024.The maturity in the Partnership allowed OGP to move from open government as a theoretical concept to something that was practiced by real people on the ground and was having a tangible impact.
* A key communications product that helped raise awareness of open government over these years has been Open Gov Week (OGW). OGW has been consistently held every year since 2018 and spotlights open government activities entirely organized by country-level reformers. In 2025, more than 40 countries organized over 2,000 events, bringing together government officials, civil society, experts and citizens to advance open government initiatives through public debates, assemblies, hackathons, webinars, and sharing stories and good practices. (Sida notes the example is from 2025, but believes it gives an insight into the magnitude of the annual Open Gov Week.)
LESSONS LEARNED related to Grant Objective 6: The past five years have demonstrated that strategic investments in communications yield measurable results in visibility, engagement, and influence. By adapting messages to global challenges, amplifying reformers voices, and improving our existing platforms, OGP has strengthened its role as a trusted and relevant platform to advance open government and its values worldwide. A key lesson from this period has been the value of storytelling as both a visibility and an influence tool. Resources dedicated to storytelling, particularly videos (for example documentary style videos) have been instrumental in spotlighting reformers and inspiring others across government and civil society.
Conclusion: Sida assesses the achieved results as overall very satisfying for the implementation period 2019-24.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
